newsitem.title: USA: U.S. industrial output dropped in October.
newsitem.headline: U.S. industrial output dropped in October.

text.p: Strikes that shut auto plants in Canada and the United States caused the first decline in U.S. industrial output in seven months during October, the Federal Reserve said on Friday.

Total output by the nation's factories, mines and utilities fell 0.5 percent last month after rising a revised 0.3 percent in September -- the first monthly falloff since a 0.5 percent drop last March.
"Sharp drops in the production of motor vehicles and in the output of related parts and materials accounted for the decrease in the overall index," the Fed said.

General Motors Corp.'s plants were hit by strikes in October that shut some assembly plants and caused shortages of parts. The rate of auto assemblies plunged to 5.5 million a year in October from 6.5 million in September, although light-truck output held steady at a 5.4 million-unit rate.
Partly as a result, businesses operated at only 82.7 percent of their maximum capacity in October, down from a revised 83.4 percent in September, the lowest rate since 82.6 percent in March.
Manufacturintg output fell 0.5 percent in October after rising 0.3 percent in September. It was the first decline in production by manufacturers since last March, when it fell 0.9 percent.
Mines and utilities also were weak last month.

Mining output dropped 1 percent after a 0.1 percent decline in September while utilities, which had been forecast to show a pickup in output, were flat in October after rising 0.3 percent in September.

Previously, the Fed said that industrial production had risen only 0.2 percent in September but it revised that up. It said capacity use was at 83.3 percent in September and also pushed it up fractionally.
The slump in motor vehicle assemblies affected all major components of manufacturing.
Output of business equipment, which had posted steady and sizeable monthly gains since May, edged up only 0.2 percent in October after a 0.8 percent September rise.
The Fed pointed out that, excluding motor vehicles, business equipment production rose a sturdy 0.7 percent, led by another sharp increase in computer output.
Analysts said the industrial production report suggested a broad-based pullback in national manufacturing activity.
"I'm struck by the across-the-board weakness in this report," said economist John Lonski at Moody's in New York.
Economist Tim McGee of Tokai Bank Ltd. in New York said the strikes at GM clearly had a major impact but he added that a more cautious consumer also was making industry slow down.

"It mainly shows that after the production spurt we had in response to the strong consumer earlier this year, production has started to slow down as a result of the consumer slowing back down," McGee said.

On Thursday the Commerce Department said sales by retail stores during October edged up only 0.2 percent after a 0.8 percent jump in September. Analysts said that raised questions whether an anticipated strong holiday shopping season between Thanksgiving and Christmas will come to pass.
